title: India's First Private Orbital Rocket Is on the Launchpad. A Billion-Dollar Bet Rides on It.
excerpt: Skyroot Aerospace, now valued at $1.1 billion with backing from Alphabet's Ram Shriram, GIC, and BlackRock, is weeks from attempting what no Indian private company has done.
body:
At a spaceport on the southeastern coast of Andhra Pradesh, a 23-metre rocket sits in its final stages of integration. Vikram-1, named after Vikram Sarabhai — the father of India's space programme — is not an ISRO creation. It was designed, built, and tested by a Hyderabad startup staffed largely by engineers who left ISRO to do what the government agency never let them: move fast.

Skyroot Aerospace, India's first space tech unicorn, is now weeks from attempting the country's first privately developed orbital launch. If it succeeds, India joins an exclusive club of nations where private companies can reach orbit. If it fails, a billion-dollar valuation and half a decade of promises reset overnight.

## The Money Behind the Rocket

In May, Skyroot closed a $60 million round that valued the company at $1.1 billion on a pre-money basis — a figure that more than doubled its previous valuation. The lead investors read like a who's who of global capital: GIC (Singapore's sovereign wealth fund), Sherpalo Ventures (founded by Ram Shriram, an Alphabet board member and early Google backer), and BlackRock.

Shriram's involvement carries symbolic weight. An Indian-American who helped build the most valuable technology company on Earth, he is now backing a bet that India can build rockets to match. He has joined Skyroot's board.

The round brought total capital raised to $160 million. The company said proceeds will scale Vikram-1 launch operations, expand manufacturing at its 200,000-square-foot Max-Q campus in Hyderabad, and accelerate development of Vikram-2 — a more powerful vehicle with a cryogenic upper stage capable of carrying one tonne to low Earth orbit.

## The Technical Stakes

Vikram-1 is designed to deliver up to 350 kilograms to low Earth orbit — comparable to Rocket Lab's Electron and Firefly Aerospace's Alpha. Its four-stage architecture includes solid-fuelled first through third stages and a hypergolic liquid upper stage (four Raman-I engines) for precise orbital injection. Skyroot claims the rocket can be assembled and launched within 24 hours, a turnaround time that would make it competitive for the dedicated small-satellite launch market.

The company completed its pre-flight integrated test campaign in April, flagging off the rocket from Hyderabad to the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota with a ceremony led by Telangana's Chief Minister. But orbital rocketry is merciless. As of late June, neither Skyroot nor its Chennai-based rival Agnikul Cosmos has completed a successful commercial orbital mission. Skyroot's 2022 sub-orbital launch of Vikram-S proved the technology; Vikram-1 must prove the business.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

India's government has set an ambitious target: expand the country's space industry from $8.4 billion today to $44 billion by 2033, roughly 8 per cent of the global space economy. Private launch capability is essential to that plan, especially as ISRO has suffered consecutive orbital launch failures.

For NRI investors and professionals, the story has direct relevance. Skyroot's co-founders Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka are IIT Kharagpur graduates who left ISRO to build the company. The investor roster — Temasek, GIC, BlackRock, the Greenko Group founders — offers public-market exposure to India's space ambitions once the company inevitably lists. And the broader ecosystem it anchors — 200-plus registered space startups, an IN-SPACe regulatory body that has liberalised access to ISRO infrastructure, and partnerships like Skyroot's MoU with Axiom Space — creates a new corridor for diaspora capital and talent.

The rocket is on the pad. Now it has to fly.
